title: Secondary neutron beam production at Jefferson Lab
summary: We investigate secondary neutron production by an 11 GeV electron beam in the Hall A beam dump at Jefferson Lab and their transport to a downstream experimental area. This secondary beam could operate opportunistically with the primary electron-scattering programme. The neutron energy spectrum extends from thermal energies to several GeVs, offering a distinctive opportunity for irradiation at energy grater than 1 GeV. We considered three configurations: the current setup, the planned BDX facility, and an optimized BDX layout with a dedicated neutron extraction pipe. We also studied how radiators made of different materials and placed upstream of the beam dump increase neutron production.

title: Stable, High-Charge, Laser-Driven VHEE Beams for Preclinical Applications
summary: Laser-driven plasma accelerators (LPAs) are promising sources of very-high-energy-electron (VHEE) beams for medical applications, but increasing charge per pulse while maintaining pointing stability remains challenging. We demonstrate laser-accelerated beams with total charge per pulse reaching (559 $\pm$ 56) pC using an 80 TW laser system. The spectra have a dominant component at 40-60 MeV and a high-energy tail extending to approximately 200 MeV. Pointing jitter measured in air at the irradiation target plane reaches as low as 0.7 mrad. The beams were used for VHEE irradiation experiments involving a 10 mm region of interest through a 40 mm depth at 400 $\pm$ 20 mGy/pulse. Spectral reproducibility is quantified over fixed-setting shot sequences. Particle-in-cell simulations produce a peak-and-tail spectrum through acceleration in successive bubbles associated with a strongly modified plasma wake, providing a plausible mechanism for maintaining substantial accelerated charge despite strong beam loading. Dose-weighted time-of-flight calculations indicate an effective pulse dose rate of $10^{12}$ Gy/s and average dose rates of tens of Gy/min. These results establish an LPA operating regime relevant to preclinical VHEE irradiation.

title: Portable Glass-RPC Telescope for Muography and Future Applications at Laser Wake Field Accelerators
summary: We report a 2025 beam test at ELBA, the multi-GeV laser wakefield accelerator at ELI Beamlines, using a Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) telescope with an active area of 16 * 16 cm2. The portable design sup- ports autonomous operation in challenging environments. Previous cosmic-ray measurements established its tracking capability for muography. During the campaign at ELBA, 30 f s long, 0.5 PW laser pulses in- teracted with a plasma target at a 0.2 Hz repetition rate, where a tungsten converter upstream of the beam dump enhanced muon production. This was the first deployment of an RPC telescope in a high-power laser environment. The detector remained operational in the presence of radiation and electromagnetic interference. Although parasitic running and limited statistics prevented definitive identification of beam- induced muons, the measurements offered insight into background activity and showed evidence of re- constructed tracks. They establish the feasibility of a dedicated campaign with controlled beam conditions and improved muon sensitivity. This contribution forms part of the International Muography Workshop 2026 proceedings.

title: Independent nuclear charge radius determinations: bound-electron $g$ factor versus muonic atom spectroscopy
summary: We present an alternative method to determine absolute nuclear charge radii competitively via the bound electron $g$ factor of H-like ions. The method is demonstrated for $^{118}$Sn by extracting its radius with a precision of 0.1%. This is the second most precise radius ever determined from an electronic system. We benchmark our result against a state-of-the-art value derived from the spectrum of muonic $^{118}$Sn. This comparison reveals a 3.2$σ$ tension, prompting a careful reexamination of the calculations and calling for additional measurements. Crucially, after decades, we now have two independent methods to measure absolute charge radii with similar precision.

title: Interface-driven second harmonic generation in indium tin oxide/gold nanolayers: density and mass discontinuities matter
summary: Second harmonic generation from transparent conductive oxides and metals is traditionally attributed to Coulomb, magnetic Lorentz, and convective sources. We show that this picture is incomplete in deeply subwavelength indium tin oxide/gold bilayers. Measurements reveal two robust spectral features, a broad maximum near 1000 nm and an epsilon-near-zero peak near 1350 nm, that persist across wide variations in material and excitation parameters. Hydrodynamic-Maxwell simulations identify an interface-specific convective mechanism activated by freeelectron density and effective-mass discontinuities at the oxide-metal boundary. As electronic homogenization develops across the bilayer, the response evolves toward one described by conventional Coulomb, Lorentz, and leading convective terms. These results establish second harmonic generation as a sensitive probe of interface-driven nonlinearities and suggest a broader role for electronic discontinuities in shaping nonlinear optical processes at surface and buried material interfaces.

title: Reconstructing intracell polarization with calibrated sapphire-window optics for collimated blue-light generation in a rubidium cell
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to JOSA B
summary: We study the polarization dependence of collimated blue light (CBL) generated near 420~nm by resonant four-wave mixing in thermal rubidium vapor in a sapphire-window cell driven at 780 and 776~nm. Sapphire windows can transform the polarization of pump light before it reaches the vapor, complicating the interpretation of polarization-dependent nonlinear emission. We measured the 780-nm pump Stokes state at an external before-cell reference plane to calibrate the common HWP/QWP preparation optics and recorded 266 off-resonant external output Stokes states after the complete sapphire-window rubidium cell at 90, 100, and 110~$^\circ$C in two propagation orientations. Direct paired-wavelength measurements show a mean before-cell 780/776 separation of $4.29^\circ$ and temperature- and orientation-specific complete-cell rotations of $22.20^\circ$--$32.02^\circ$, with rms residuals of $4.83^\circ$--$12.87^\circ$. Using this calibrated co-prepared pump description, we analyzed 2574 measurements of total spectrally filtered 420-nm CBL intensity. Across the six temperature--orientation data sets, a complete nine-coefficient second-order response yielded cross-validated $R^2$ values of 0.636 to 0.828. These paired-wavelength measurements establish, for each temperature--orientation data set, a fixed relative Stokes-space map between the two co-prepared pump trajectories, with the residual of this mapping defining the experimental uncertainty of the correlated two-pump reduction used in the response model. Thus, the resulting framework combines a reconstructed vapor-entrance polarization coordinate with direct two-wavelength calibration of the assembled cell and provides a practical basis for polarization-controlled nonlinear-optical experiments in sapphire-window vapor cells.

title: Motion-Induced Polaron Resonance beyond the Orthogonality Catastrophe
summary: We investigate the spectroscopic response of a repulsively interacting, infinitely heavy impurity moving at constant velocity $v$ through a one-dimensional ideal Fermi gas. Using an exact functional-determinant approach, we calculate the Ramsey response and spectral function, fully accounting for many-body particle-hole excitations. We uncover a strongly nonmonotonic dependence on impurity velocity: decoherence is enhanced around the Fermi velocity, whereas sufficiently rapid motion restores a narrow, long-lived polaron resonance. A long-time wave-packet analysis yields analytical expressions for the polaron energy and decay rate over the full velocity range and quantitatively captures the numerical results. At high velocity, the polaron energy approaches the mean-field value, the decay rate vanishes as $1/v$, and the spectral weight approaches unity. Thus, rapid prescribed motion provides a dynamical route to suppressing the orthogonality catastrophe and restoring polaron coherence even for an infinitely heavy impurity, where recoil is entirely absent.

title: From spectroscopy to quantum dynamics: assessing reduced models of a NaCs molecular gate
summary: We investigate how spectroscopic calibration and basis selection affect predictions for a dipolar-exchange gate between two optically trapped $^{23}$Na$^{133}$Cs molecules. We construct a 128-state molecular Hamiltonian restricted to the $N=0,1$ rotational manifold, fit two effective optical parameters to three bright microwave transitions, and compare the resulting spectrum with four additional lines. In the coherent pair model, changing the optical polarization angle by $+0.1^\circ$ reduces the calculated gate fidelity from 94.64\% to 1.09\% at fixed carrier frequencies. Retuning the carriers and restoring the target Rabi frequencies recovers 89.31\%. The remaining sensitivity reflects changes in the multilevel pair dynamics that are not removed by target-frequency and target-Rabi recalibration. Enlarging the molecular basis produces nonmonotonic changes in fidelity, although the 11-state and 25-state calculations give closely agreeing logical maps after phase alignment. Two controls with isolated transfer probabilities near 98.45\% yield complete-gate fidelities differing by more than 11 percentage points. We relate these comparisons to a sufficient bound on the error of a projected propagator. The numerical tests quantify agreement among selected bases for a specified coherent Hamiltonian.

title: Complex Hyperspin Machine and Symmetry Quenching: Benchmark and scaling up to millions of degrees of freedom
summary: Driven-dissipative oscillator networks have been proposed to simulate spin models on physical hardware, mostly focusing on systems of binary (Ising) spins, or systems of spin vectors in low dimensions. The equalized hyperspin machine was recently introduced to provide a single platform to simulate general models of $N$ coupled spin vectors with tunable dimension $D$, realizing dynamical annealing protocols to vary the spin dimensionality in time. These schemes are limited to real spins coupled via real coupling matrices. We propose a generalization of the hyperspin machine that works with complex fields and deals with complex Hermitian coupling matrices, implementing an amplitude equalization scheme. This system, which we name complex hyperspin machine, can work on optimization problems with complex valued hyperspins that can be cast on complex $D$-vector Hamiltonians. We benchmark the machine against a differential evolution (DE) algorithm on complex $D=2$ hyperspins up to $N=80$, showing that the fraction of instances where a lower-energy solution is found grows with system size and coupling density, reaching $92.5\%$ at the largest considered sizes. When the DE finds a lower-energy solution, the machine still reaches a median relative energy deviation that lies between $10^{-15}$ and $10^{-12}$ while running at substantially lower computational cost. Using the complex nature of the field, we introduce a new dimensional reduction protocol that we name symmetry quenching, which collapses complex variables that map to XY spins onto real Ising spins by switching on the parametric pump. We show on Max-Cut instances with known ground states that symmetry quenching outperforms a fixed-pump Ising machine, reaching exact ground states in the presence of equalization. We scale the system to $N=10^6$ hyperspins, or $8\times10^6$ dynamical variables, on a Hermitian sparse two-dimensional lattice.

title: Scalable Unitary State-Encoding for Generic Large Data
summary: Efficient encoding of data into quantum states remains a fundamental bottleneck in many quantum computing protocols, which would otherwise offer advantages over their classical counterparts. Here, we introduce deterministic and scalable amplitude-encoding methods with low two-qubit gate costs and tunable trade-offs between circuit depth and encoding fidelity. Our approaches require no amplitude amplification or mid-circuit measurement and are capable of encoding arbitrary complex data or queryable functions by using tensor-networks to go beyond what can be held in classical memory. Our principle contributions are two complementary algorithms for simplifying fully controlled multiplexer circuits to one- and two-qubit gates. In the first, we formally map the elimination of redundant gate controls to a Boolean logic minimization problem, while in the second we utilize a single ancilla qubit to map the multi-controlled rotation gates to a sequence of one- and two-qubit operations via the Walsh-Hadamard spectrum of the gate angles. We benchmark these methods across a broad range of function classes, characterizing their total depth in an all-to-all connectivity graph against system size and target fidelity. Hybridizing our methods gives up to orders of magnitude improvement in circuit depth at equivalent state fidelity compared to the default state-preparation method in the Qiskit package. We furthermore demonstrate our method on IQM hardware with a square lattice connectivity, finding excellent fidelity, even with minimal noise mitigation. By significantly reducing gate depth for encoding, this work enables the experimental execution of applications on current and near-term hardware which would otherwise be reduced to noise before the first calculation step, shortening the time horizon to robust quantum utility.

title: SparseModesNet for coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical system in heterogeneous porous media
summary: Coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) models describe interactions among displacement, fluid pressure, and temperature in geothermal systems. Fine-mesh simulations over many time steps are costly, particularly with heterogeneous permeability and thermal conductivity or fracture networks that alter fluid and heat transport. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) reduces the number of unknowns but can require many modes because its reconstruction is linear. We apply SparseModesNet to reconstruct coupled THM solutions using a small set of selected modes and a neural-network nonlinear decoder. Starting from a larger collection of candidate modes, SparseModesNet selects modes to reduce reconstruction error rather than simply retaining those with the highest energy. We compare SparseModesNet with POD on three problems: a two-dimensional heterogeneous medium, a two-dimensional connected fracture network, and a three-dimensional geometry based on Utah FORGE fractures. We evaluate reconstructed displacement, pressure, and temperature fields, as well as pressure- and temperature-based quantities of interest. We also test temporal interpolation by training on a subset of snapshots and reconstructing omitted snapshots within the same time interval. For the same reduced dimension, SparseModesNet achieves smaller reconstruction errors than POD and accurately recovers the solution fields and selected geothermal quantities of interest.

title: Physics Informed Priors for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials with Uncertainty Quantification
summary: Standard uncertainty quantification methods for machine learning interatomic potentials often fail to quantify the effects of model misspecification despite its prominence as a source of error. To combat this, misspecification-aware uncertainty schemes have been gaining attention, pointwise optimal parameter set regression (POPS-Regression) among them. However, no guarantees on the physicality of the posterior distribution are given and uncertainty estimates can be conservative compared to the true error. To combat this, we present a model misspecification aware scheme that builds on POPS-Regression by allowing users to specify physical priors that are enforced across the obtained ensemble of models. This allows the user to incorporate misspecification-aware uncertainties without compromising on physical properties. The scheme is applicable to any physical quantity that can be represented by a convex set of parameters and so is robust for a wide variety of static properties which can help inform dynamical simulations. Here, we demonstrate the scheme for phononic vibrations and elastic properties. The scheme is also applied to both linear and message-passing neural network potentials by exploiting the linearity available in both architectures; for neural network potentials we approximate the readout layer as a linear model based on fixed non-linear features. The versatility of the method provides an alternative to hand-crafted or active learning approaches to data-set construction to correct physical failures by adding data thus reducing the computational overhead for designing potentials for specific applications.

title: Low-Rank Iteration for Efficient Calculations of Topological Surface States
summary: Surface states are hallmarks of topological phases, and their efficient computation is crucial for topology characterization. Conventional supercell methods (SCM) approximate semi-infinite systems as finite periodic ones, but suffer from high computational cost, artificial inter-surface coupling, and slow convergence near band edges. Recently, boundary problems for semi-infinite systems have been recast as block-tridiagonal equations and solved by the cyclic reduction method (CRM) and the transfer matrix method (TMM). However, these approaches remain resource-intensive, as fine-mesh discretization produces very large matrices. Recognizing the intrinsic sparsity and low rank of these matrices, we develop a low-rank iterative method (LIM) with stochastic trace estimation that substantially reduces complexity and memory without sacrificing accuracy, while remaining straightforwardly parallelizable. Benchmarks on 2D and 3D topological systems show orders-of-magnitude acceleration over CRM and TMM. LIM extends readily to heterostructures, defective interfaces, and non-Hermitian systems, providing an efficient platform for topological and plasmonic surface phenomena.

title: A Quantum Mechanical Description of Active Matter
summary: The natural environments habitable to life are inseparable from dissipative and entropic forces, which mandate active matter to operate on constant fluxes of energy and momentum to survive and propagate through spacetime. In contrast to fundamental particles which are characterized by energy and momentum, we postulate that energy expenditure rate and momentum generation rate are the fundamental dynamical quantities driving this evolution of swimming active matter and accordingly construct the corresponding Lagrangian and Hamiltonian of motion of the active matter. Furthermore, living systems broadly employ periodic, non-repeating motion for both locomotion and various biological functions, with meaningful information stored in the periods of these functions. Consequently, analyzing these dynamics in the Fourier space lands us at the familiar tools of the operator based, quantum mechanics. This is accomplished by introducing a complex field to describe the evolving probability distribution of a single unit, as well as the population density of mutually non-interacting active particles under the constraint of scarce resources. The resulting single-unit wavefunction evolves analogously to the Dirac equation with minimal coupling, wherein gauge symmetry reflects the generality of the governing equations across arbitrary resource landscapes. Additionally, we present a Schrödinger-like equation where the effective potential term represents the environmentally mandated, non-motile base metabolic rate. Finally, we formalize the bidirectional coupling between active swimmers and the surrounding fluid via a multipole expansion of the active force with an emphasis on force monopoles and dipoles, where each pole corresponds to a distinct mode of active motility.

title: Enforcing Symmetries on Pre-trained ML Models for Physics
summary: Post-hoc group averaging (or test-time augmentation) is a simple way to impose symmetry on a trained predictor without changing its architecture or retraining it. For finite and compact groups, averaging over a normalized Haar measure on the group gives the Reynolds operator: a canonical projection onto invariant or equivariant predictors with known non-increasing risk guarantees under certain assumptions. This paper provides numerical experiments on physics emulation models that demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in this setting. We then extend this framework to non-compact group symmetries. For non-compact groups, the Haar measure cannot be normalized, so group averaging cannot be defined in the same way. We replace it with three alternatives: the Weyl unitary trick (which requires complexifying the space and extending the predictor), a data-dependent orthogonal projection (which involves a non-trivial optimization on the space of invariant or equivariant functions), and a frame averaging approach (which involves mapping each point to a set of orbit representatives). We illustrate the constructions theoretically and empirically on the unit-rescaling group and the Lorentz group. Our results show that in the non-compact case, the Weyl trick and frame averaging do not provide a consistent improvement over the baseline, except where the test data is out-of-distribution (an orders-of-magnitude improvement in this case) and, for the Weyl trick, in low-data regimes. The orthogonal projection can provide improvements in-distribution and out-of-distribution. We also observe that models trained directly on invariant features matched or beat the projection of an unconstrained one. We conclude that post-hoc symmetrization extends to non-compact groups, but it does not consistently outperform training a symmetric model.

title: Quantifying the importance of equation of state and transport property compatibility in supercritical fluids
comment: Submitted to Journal of Supercritical Fluids
summary: High-fidelity simulation of supercritical flows requires accurate values of thermodynamic properties including the density (rho), specific heat cp, enthalpy h, and entropy s as well as transport properties such as the viscosity (eta) and thermal conductivity (lambda) as functions of the temperature T and pressure P. In simulations of mixtures, such as supercritical carbon dioxide (sCO2) with contaminants, a generalized equation of state (EoS) is often used, leading to errors in rho(T,P) when compared to results from correlations developed specifically for individual species. Similarly, generalized correlations for eta and lambda are often used, with a corresponding decrease in accuracy. However, a second source of error is introduced in calculations of transport properties. These correlations are created and computed as functions of T and rho instead of as functions of T and P. Because of this, when eta(T,rho )and lambda(T,rho) are calculated, errors in rho(T,P) propagate through the calculation. This work creates a procedure for tracking both errors caused by using a generalized correlation for eta(T,rho) and lambda(T,rho), and for tracking the errors caused by using a generalized correlation for rho(T,P) in these calculations. The viscosity and thermal conductivity of supercritical CO2, N2, andCH4 are used as examples to demonstrate how to separate the errors due to the generalized property correlations and the errors due to the generalized EoS. Both sources of error are largest near the critical temperature Tc. These errors are large enough to impact both the numeric stability and the accuracy of simulations.

title: Electrohydrodynamic interactions of two Quincke rotors: asymptotic theory and boundary element simulations
summary: Weakly conducting spheres suspended in a leaky dielectric fluid can undergo spontaneous Quincke rotation when the applied electric field exceeds a critical value. We investigate how electric and hydrodynamic interactions modify this instability and the subsequent rotation of two spheres at fixed separation and orientation. Starting from electric dipole and hydrodynamic rotlet interactions, we develop a systematic far-field asymptotic theory. Away from onset, slow drift of the rotation axes makes a regular expansion fail at long times. A multiple-scale expansion gives slow phase equations that select the axes according to pair orientation and field strength. Near onset, weak interactions produce corrections comparable to the isolated rotation magnitude. A detuned multiple-scale expansion gives coupled equations for the transverse dipole amplitudes. Their linearization identifies four collective rotation modes, whose critical fields and steady branches with one active mode are determined together with their stability. At leading order near onset, electric interaction shifts all four modal thresholds equally, whereas hydrodynamic interaction makes counter-rotation appear first for pair angles below $\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)\simeq54.7^\circ$ and co-rotation above it. Away from onset, the angle separating stable counter-rotation from stable co-rotation increases with field strength. Boundary element method (BEM) simulations place onset within a field interval for each configuration and resolve the growth and relaxation of rotation. Steady-speed comparisons show how pair orientation changes the balance between electric and hydrodynamic effects. We compare the unexpanded dipole-rotlet model of Das and Saintillan [Phys. Rev. E 87, 043014 (2013)] with our asymptotic theory and BEM simulations.

title: Bathyspheres, dust devils, lunar plumes and Martian drones: a generalised mathematical model for particle-fluid flow fields generated by static particle bed entrainment across macroscopic scales
summary: We consider a recently derived mathematical model for the mechanism by which a wind driven flow entrains particles into a fluid from an otherwise static particle bed, a process that is fundamental in initiating and driving the phenomenon of particle cloud formation. This model was previously applied to the "helicopter brownout" problem, in which, as a helicopter descends towards a bed of sand, the downwash and swirling flow from the rotors entrain particles into the air, forming a high-velocity particle-laden cloud around the helicopter. Here, we define a new measure of particle cloud formation potential, outline how the model can be incorporated into existing Computational Fluid Dynamics software, and extend the model to scenarios including: formation of particle clouds in the absence of swirl, such as those caused by a bathysphere descending to the ocean bed, or a rocket landing on the lunar surface, in which case we can precisely predict the critical height above the surface at which particle cloud formation is initiated; generation of dust clouds by less powerful downwash and swirling flows caused by drones or other smaller rotorcraft, such as NASA's Ingenuity Mars helicopter, in which case gravitational effects are included in the model; formation of dust devils (dust clouds formed within and around an upwardly circulating columnar air flow), in which case downwash is replaced by updraft. In each case, predictive models are derived through minor adaptations to key modelling assumptions.

title: Immobilisation and remobilisation of surfactant-covered drop interfaces in electric fields: Simulations
summary: Fluid--fluid interfaces are seldom clean due to the presence of surfactants, which can strongly modify their dynamics. Interfacial flow redistributes surfactant, creating concentration gradients whose Marangoni stresses can immobilise the interface. By contrast, surface diffusion or exchange with the bulk can reduce these gradients and restore interfacial motion. We study this competition using a two-dimensional model of a surfactant-covered leaky-dielectric drop in a uniform electric field. Electric stresses drive the classical Taylor circulation, in which the drop remains non-rotating. At stronger fields, convection of interfacial charge can destabilise this state and produce the Quincke regime, characterised by spontaneous mean rotation. Using a fully nonlinear model on a fixed circular interface, we show that weak surfactant diffusion allows Marangoni stresses to suppress the Taylor circulation almost completely. Quincke rotation remobilises this nearly arrested interface and restores a substantial straining circulation, whose orientation varies with the applied field. Surfactant also shifts the critical field for rotation and can change the onset from subcritical to supercritical. Surface diffusion and exchange with a well-mixed bulk reservoir can produce similar flow responses and rotation thresholds despite different surfactant distributions. The spatial variation of surfactant concentration therefore provides additional information for distinguishing the two transport mechanisms.

title: Radiation-driven melting and porous flow in the near-surface layer of an ice sheet
summary: The ablation area of an ice sheet can undergo melting both directly at the surface and in the metre or so below the surface, due to the penetration and absorption of shortwave radiation. The fate of the meltwater has important implications for the mass balance of the ice sheet; some of it runs off into surface streams and eventually to the ocean, while some is stored in the porous `weathering crust', and can refreeze. We present a fluid-mechanical model to analyse the downward percolation and lateral drainage of the meltwater in the crust, and its influence on porosity, saturation, temperature and melting rate. Previous models have either ignored the possibility for lateral drainage, in which case the crust is always saturated with water, or have made ad-hoc assumptions about where and how the meltwater runs off. Through a series of analytical and numerical solutions to the model, we find that lateral drainage has the effect of controlling the water table within the weathering crust, which separates an unsaturated region near the surface from a saturated aquifer beneath. Under fluctuating weather conditions that induce melting and refreezing, the lateral drainage can result in the near-surface ice being more porous and also colder than is the case without lateral drainage. The model is able to predict the partitioning of the meltwater between surface and subsurface runoff, and refreezing, and has potential to be incorporated within larger-scale models of the ice-sheet mass balance.

title: Time-gated optical-parametric-amplification and field-resolved detection of mid-infrared free-induction decay signals
summary: Infrared spectroscopy is a key tool to study complex structural dynamics in molecular systems. However, resolving weak or broad vibrational modes is challenging due to their rapid decay. Here, we demonstrate a technique to significantly extend the detectable lifetime - and thereby spectral resolution - of molecular signatures by employing synchronized time-gated optical parametric amplification of mid-infrared free-induction decay signals. Utilizing a Cr:ZnS laser system and a nonlinear ZnGeP2 crystal, we achieve a 10-fold increase in the electric field strength of the infrared molecular signal, yielding a two-orders of magnitude enhancement in dynamic range and a 2-fold increase in the signal-to-noise ratio. Using isopropyl alcohol as a model system, we demonstrate that OPA-enhanced detection extends the observable window of vibrational modes up to 72 %. This approach allows for the reconstruction of high-fidelity molecular fingerprints that resolve complex vibrational relaxation pathways and weak structural dynamics, previously hidden within the background and noise, providing a pathway for new high-sensitivity and time-resolved studies of complex chemical structures.

title: Transformer-Based Characterization of Criticality in Directed Percolation
summary: Directed percolation (DP) provides a canonical framework for studying nonequilibrium phase transitions into absorbing states, yet extracting critical behavior directly from high-dimensional spatiotemporal configurations remains challenging. Here, we investigate (1 + 1)- and (2 + 1)-dimensional bond DP using a supervised Transformer encoder. Supervised learning results demonstrate that the Transformer can distinguish between the active and absorbing phases of directed percolation with high accuracy. The critical point and critical exponents estimated from the model's classification probabilities align closely with reference values from existing literature, indicating that the model not only achieves phase classification but also yields outputs containing information related to critical scaling behavior. To probe the model's internal representation, we employ attention rollout and define an attention center that quantifies the temporal centroid of the cumulative attention distribution. The attention patterns and the attention center reorganize systematically near the critical region and exhibit pronounced finite-size dependence. Finally, we examined the model's transferability between configurations generated from fully occupied initial states and those from single-seed initial states. The results indicate the presence of transferable information between the two types of data, though the transfer performance exhibits directional asymmetry. Furthermore, when using an equal amount of target-domain data, fine-tuning yielded only a marginal improvement in accuracy compared to training from scratch.

title: Turbulent wakes behind nine bluff-body shapes from direct numerical simulation and particle image velocimetry
summary: We present a cross-validated dataset of turbulent wakes behind nine bluff bodies at Reynolds number Re = 10,000: a circular cylinder, a 2:1 elliptical cylinder at 0° and 90°, short and long isosceles triangles with the apex upstream or downstream, and a square cylinder at 0° and 45°. Each body was studied by wall-resolved direct numerical simulation (DNS) with a spectral-element solver and by time-resolved planar particle image velocimetry (PIV) in the MIT Intelligent Towing Tank. The DNS records contain time- and spanwise-averaged velocity, pressure and Reynolds stresses, 24-bin phase-averaged fields keyed to the lift signal, drag and lift histories, and one three-dimensional instantaneous snapshot per body; the PIV records contain the matching time-mean and phase-averaged fields in the same coordinate frame. The DNS set-up is verified against reference cylinder data at Re = 3900, and DNS and PIV at Re = 10,000 are compared field by field. The dataset supports the development and testing of data-driven turbulence closures, reduced-order models, and wake-stability analyses across geometries with distinct separation behavior.

title: Probing injection locking of an integrated nanolaser pair through RF beating
summary: We demonstrate simultaneous optical injection locking of an integrated pair of photonic-crystal nanolasers coupled to a common silicon waveguide. Due to fabrication-induced disorder, the two nanolasers exhibit distinct emission wavelengths, allowing their individual locking ranges to be resolved as a function of the injection-laser detuning and power. We identify a region where both nanolasers are simultaneously locked to the master laser. To probe this collective locked state, the two nanolasers are independently pump-modulated at distinct radio frequencies. A beat note at the difference frequency appears only within the overlap region, providing a direct RF signature of simultaneous locking. These results establish RF beating as a compact diagnostic of common-master injection locking in integrated nanolaser systems.

title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates
summary: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.

title: Vertically-coupled microring resonators for lithium niobate on insulator integrated photonics
summary: We propose and demonstrate lithium niobate on insulator (LNOI) microring resonators that are verticallycoupled to index-matched silicon-rich silicon nitride (SiN x ) access waveguides as an alternative to conventional lateral coupling schemes for integrated photonics applications. The wafer-scalable fabrication process involves a planarization step exploiting a single-step and reproducible spin-coating of a SU-8 epoxy spacer layer which allows a controlled separation to be established between the resonator and its access waveguide. The resulting multimode and single-mode microring resonators exhibit, for their fundamental TE 0 mode, intrinsic quality factors of 4.0 x 10 5 and 3.4 x 10 5 , respectively.

title: Are the tearing and the Weibel instabilities the same?
summary: The tearing instability, which extracts free energy from a magnetic field gradient, and the Weibel instability, which draws free energy from temperature anisotropies, appear at first glance to be fundamentally distinct. However, the magnetic field gradient in the tearing instability requires a current, and the resulting plasma drift leads to an effective temperature anisotropy, so that the plasma is hotter along the direction of the current flow. This anisotropy can play an essential role in driving the instability. We demonstrate, using semi-implicit particle-in-cell simulations, a smooth transition between the tearing regime for thick current sheets, where the anisotropy has little influence, and a thin-current-sheet regime better described by Weibel physics. We find that for current sheet thicknesses less than the ion Larmor radius, where standard assumptions of the tearing instability break down, the growth rate of the mode commonly identified as the tearing instability agrees remarkably well with the growth rate predicted by ion-cyclotron theory, which is essentially the magnetized counterpart of the Weibel instability.

title: Mode interaction in inclined-layer convection: a physical interpretation
summary: We carry out a numerical investigation of the Oberbeck--Boussinesq equations in a fluid layer inclined against gravity. Equilibria containing different numbers of co-rotating rolls are computed. Mixed-mode branches connect branches containing states with four and six identical co-rotating rolls. These branches display two contrasting routes to reducing (or increasing) the number of rolls, one in which rolls disappear (or appear) and another route in which rolls merge (or split). These results are interpreted in light of the $(2,3)$ mode interaction scenario.

title: Magnon-polaritons in terahertz resonators based on antiferromagnets with weak ferromagnetism
summary: Terahertz magnon-polaritons in antiferromagnets with weak ferromagnetism are theoretically investigated using YFeO$_3$ as an example. Dispersion relations are obtained for the quasi-ferromagnetic and quasi-antiferromagnetic modes. It is shown that the intrinsic Fabry--Perot resonances of the magnetic slab provide strong coupling, but their low quality factor limits the cooperativity. The photonic crystal cavity increases the cooperativity of the quasi-antiferromagnetic mode from $C\sim6$ to $C\sim41$ at 300K and to $2.2\times10^3$ at 63K.

title: Different exact-law formulations to calculate the energy cascade rate in magnetohydrodynamic turbulence with and without mean magnetic fields
summary: At scales much larger than the ion inertial length and ion-gyroscale, space-plasma turbulence is often described within the framework of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics (MHD). Using high-resolution direct numerical simulations with $1024^3$ grid points, we perform the first systematic numerical comparison of three exact-law formulations for the total energy cascade in homogeneous, but not necessarily isotropic, MHD turbulence: the Yaglom-Monin (YM), Banerjee-Galtier (BG), and two-point correlator formulations. Despite directional variations, the angle-averaged energy transfer rates for all three formulations show excellent agreement for zero, moderate, and strong background magnetic fields. These results clearly suggest the usefulness of alternative BG and correlator formulations for estimating the energy cascade rates in turbulent space plasmas when the required spatial derivatives are accessible through multi-spacecraft measurements. We also argue that the isotropic Politano-Pouquet (PP) formulation does not provide a true directional transfer rate and therefore its application as a single-direction energy transfer rate estimator leads to inaccurate values, especially under anisotropic conditions. Decomposing the exact formulations into RMHD and non-RMHD contributions, we also show that the RMHD cascade rates cannot be obtained merely by increasing the strength of the mean magnetic field in incompressible magnetohydrodynamic turbulence. Finally, a term-by-term analysis of different formulations reveals how different nonlinear interaction channels coexist and collaborate with each other to maintain the same energy cascade rate across the inertial scales.

title: Selection versus residuals: deep-learning solvers for the Dubreil-Jacotin-Long equation and application to mode-2 internal solitary waves
summary: Neural solvers offer structural flexibility for the Dubreil-Jacotin--Long (DJL) equation of internal solitary waves, which also admits the trivial state, oscillatory wavetrains and broadened near-solutions. A solver must select the physical wave before resolving it. Turkington's variational principle selects the wave through the nonlinearity of the available potential energy (APE). An exact virial partition shows that every localized wave carries more kinetic energy than APE, so a quadratic APE would favour a broadened field. The nonlinear APE enhancement, $1.27$--$2.06\times$ for the computed waves, reverses this ordering, although the preferred width remains weakly selected. From a shared KdV-derived start, a constrained Deep Ritz objective recovers the mode-1 wave, whereas strong- and weak-form residual objectives, which vanish at every exact solution and therefore do not favour the physical wave over other roots, lose the prescribed APE within one descent round. The recovered wave is under-resolved because its residual is dominated by high-wavenumber error that the energy barely penalizes, and a residual refinement at exact APE then meets every acceptance criterion. Structurally excluding mode 1 from the trial space, we compute mode-2 waves on four stratifications. A computed wave core qualitatively reproduces the two-lobe structure observed on the South China Sea shelf. In the deep basin, the selected core misses the residual criterion, and residual refinement widens it with little change in the energy objective. The two resolved linear estimates suggest weaker relative mode-1 radiation at larger ratios of wave half-width to resonant wavelength.

title: Multipole Decomposition of Moving Sources
summary: Cartesian multipole moments are widely used to analyze and engineer radiation, but the usual relations for their radiated fields assume a wavevector-independent source frequency. For moving sources, Doppler shifts make the frequency depend on the wavevector, so the radiated fields predicted from the moments generally carry errors proportional to v/c. From charge conservation in the laboratory frame, we derive a multipole decomposition of moving sources that retains the usual moments but evaluates their contributions at Doppler-shifted wavenumbers and adds a convection-current term. Requiring no rest frame, it applies to moving matter and to excitation patterns in synthetic motion through media at rest, including superluminal ones. The decomposition also extends to nonuniform translation and to nonrigid patterns with curved spectral supports. Exact calculations for moving electric, magnetic, and toroidal dipoles confirm the decomposition and attribute the different radiation of a dipole in moving matter and in synthetic motion to the laboratory moments that each kind of motion induces. For an anapole, these moments decide whether it radiates. An anapole carried by uniformly moving matter remains nonradiating, whereas an excitation pattern with the same electric and toroidal dipoles radiates in synthetic motion. The decomposition thus makes multipolar analysis available for moving matter and for excitation patterns in synthetic motion, and it opens the way to designing their radiation.

title: Violent relaxation redux
summary: Collisionless self-gravitating systems, such as merging galaxies, have long seemed an exception to the statistical-mechanical principle that chaotic many-body systems relax to maximum-entropy states: Lynden-Bell's statistical mechanics of their "violent relaxation," constrained by exact conservation of phase-space volume -- equivalently, of infinitely many collisionless "Casimir" invariants -- has appeared not to be a good description. We propose that violent relaxation does give rise to Lynden-Bell's maximum-entropy equilibria, but that both are underpinned by gravitational turbulence, in which large-scale gravitational fluctuations drive chaotic phase-space mixing of the particles' distribution function. We derive the universal small-scale (sub-Jeans) spectra of this turbulence and show that it leads to phase-space-volume conservation being broken on a timescale only logarithmically longer, in the particle number N, than the dynamical (violent-relaxation) time. This timescale separation lets the system relax "adiabatically" through a sequence of Lynden-Bell equilibria, each corresponding to instantaneous values of the Casimirs. At long times, it approaches an equilibrium close to its "ground state": a distribution whose Casimirs have adjusted so that the system's energy is now its minimum possible energy. Thus, the system's universal tendency is toward a minimum-energy, maximum-entropy state. We corroborate this picture with 1D N-body simulations and hypothesize that it can explain the universal equilibria of galaxies and dark-matter halos.

title: Domain-Adapted Deep Optical Flow for Multiphase Velocimetry in Unsteady Cloud Cavitation
comment: 39 pages, 17 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to Experiments in Fluids
summary: Time-resolved velocimetry inside cloud cavitation remains a fundamental measurement problem. Particle image velocimetry (PIV) requires uniform tracer seeding and undistorted particle images, and cavitating flow violates both, because tracers do not penetrate vapor structures and refractive index mismatch across deforming interfaces produces spurious vectors. We present a domain-adapted deep optical flow framework for two-phase velocimetry, built on a Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms (RAFT) architecture fine-tuned on synthetic image pairs rendered from multiphase OpenFOAM simulations (RAFT-CloudCav). It is evaluated against a pre-trained generalist RAFT model, Farnebäck and OpenPIV on 130,000 frames/s recordings of a Venturi test section at 30 and 48 L/min. As no experimental ground truth exists, validation uses three quantities that require none, namely the integrated flow rate against a turbine meter, the liquid-phase velocity divergence, which mass conservation requires to vanish, and the station-to-station spread of the flow rate. RAFT-CloudCav recovers 47.75 L/min against a metered 48.0 $\pm$ 0.5 L/min, the closest of the four methods, and its flow rate varies by 2.0% across four streamwise stations, versus 6-7% for the classical methods. It returns a coherent near-wall reverse flow of -0.71 m/s, the time-averaged signature of the upstream-propagating re-entrant jet, where OpenPIV returns none. In the non-cavitating control, at 51 $μ$m/pixel only three grid points fall inside a 0.68 mm boundary layer and the peak wall-normal gradient is under-predicted more than thirtyfold, while 13 and 19 $μ$m/pixel agree with each other. The mean field is recovered without tracer particles at roughly three times the per-frame uncertainty. Uncertainties are estimated a posteriori from the image residual and propagated conservatively.

title: Layer-Peeling Inversion of Temporal Refractive Index Profiles from Noisy Data
summary: We introduce a direct method for reconstructing the temporal evolution of a medium from electromagnetic field measurements. A sequence of temporal refractive-index changes splits an incident wave into forward- and backward-propagating components, producing a \emph{spatial} response of finite extent. We show that this finite support, together with causality, enables sequential reconstruction of the temporal interfaces through a time-domain extension of layer peeling. For continuously varying media, we introduce a time-adjusted Goupillaud medium and, through space-time duality, establish the corresponding momentum-conservation and admissibility conditions. The method remains robust under incomplete and noisy measurements, providing a general framework for the metrology, characterization, and design of time-varying electromagnetic systems.

title: Existence of Distinct Strong and Weak Shear Regimes of Self-Generated Turbulent Magnetic Reconnection
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, accepted for the Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: Magnetic reconnection can become fast in three-dimensional turbulent layers. However, the parameters and mechanisms that control the fast state are not yet fully clear. Existing guide-field simulations of self-generated turbulent reconnection show locally coherent flux-rope structures embedded in a stochastic layer, motivating a flux-rope-mediated picture, with reconnection rates of order $V_{\rm rec}/V_A \sim 0.01$ in MHD. Here, we test whether and how magnetic shear changes the reconnection regime, using 3D resistive-MHD simulations at $S_L=10^5$. We vary the guide field while keeping the initial reconnecting field strength and rate normalization fixed, comparing a guide-field, weaker-shear configuration with the anti-parallel, strong-shear limit. We find that the strong-shear regime is qualitatively distinct from the flux-rope-mediated guide-field regime. Rather than retaining a narrow layer and locally coherent flux-rope structures, the current layer develops short-wavelength corrugations that broaden it substantially, and the reconnection layer electric field is sustained by fluctuation EMF. The reconnection rate increases to $V_{\rm rec}/V_A \sim 0.03$, about three times the guide-field value. These results indicate that magnetic shear can select the mechanism controlling fast 3D turbulent reconnection, shifting the system from a guide-field regime consistent with flux-rope mediation toward a very fast turbulence-broadened regime. This transition provides a novel explanation for the sudden switch-on of fast reconnection in eruptive solar flares.

title: Sub-filter-scale stress and heat flux in hypersonic Couette flow and a flat-plate boundary layer
comment: Submitted to the Journal of Fluid Mechanics; currently under review
summary: A comparative study of sub-filter-scale (SFS) quantities in hypersonic Couette flow and flat-plate boundary layer turbulence under strongly cooled-wall conditions is carried out using filtered direct numerical simulation (DNS) data to characterize the differences in SFS dynamics between internal and external wall-bounded turbulence. The two flows exhibit similar near-wall behaviour in the mean velocity profiles and SFS stress components; however, marked differences emerge in the outer layer and thermal structure. The two configurations also exhibit different thermal fields, leading to different temperature-velocity relations. The SFS behaviour shows strong sensitivity to the filtering operation: the top-hat filter yields larger SFS magnitudes, whereas the sharp spectral filter preserves a distinct spectral separation near the cutoff, leading to characteristic SFS features. Decomposition of the SFS terms shows that the residual component provides the dominant contribution to the mean SFS shear stress and heat flux. Differences between the two flows are primarily associated with the interaction terms between the resolved and residual components, which contribute with opposite signs in the two configurations, consistent with their different thermal structures. The different thermal structures also lead to distinct SFS heat-flux behaviour, including a sign change in the flat-plate boundary layer. Instantaneous SFS fields further reveal that local extrema arise from the combined contributions of multiple decomposed terms. Although these terms exhibit large local fluctuations, their net contributions to the averaged SFS quantities are relatively small. The trace of the SFS stress exhibits local negative values, reflecting local energy redistribution across the filter scale rather than a loss of physical energy.

title: A hair-thin implant opens the entire depth of the mouse brain to revisiting the same structures at subcellular resolution
comment: These authors contributed equally: Miroslav Stibůrek, Tomáš Pikálek, Petra Ondráčková Corresponding authors: Hana Uhlířová (huhlirova@isibrno.cz) and Tomáš Čižmár (cizmart@isibrno.cz)
summary: Ultrathin multimode-fibre endoscopes provide minimally invasive access to subcellular structures throughout the depth of the mouse brain. Here we introduce a chronically implantable interface with a diameter of 144 μm, about the thickness of a human hair, that extends this capability to longitudinal imaging, enabling repeated access to the same fine structures over extended periods. The system supports weeks-long tracking of individual dendritic spines, allowing quantitative comparison of their dynamics and survival across dendritic compartments. We further demonstrate longitudinal intracellular calcium imaging during spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity in the same cells across days, as well as repeated measurements of blood flow in the same vessels across multiple brain regions. This chronic endomicroscopic platform provides stable, minimally invasive optical access for longitudinal subcellular-resolution imaging of brain structure, activity and blood flow across depth.

title: An Analytical Model for Laser-Activated Two-Phase Choking and Microfluidic Suction on Surface Boundary Layers
comment: Submitted for publication. The source code used to produce Figure 2 is hosted openly at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23134296
summary: We present a predictive fluid mechanics model to calculate pressure drops (0.25 atm) and fluid velocities (2.50 m/s) governed by localized phase change and choking phenomena in a capillary-constrained, coaxial microfluidic actuator. Driven by near-infrared thermal absorption, the analytical framework describes how energy deposition drives vapor cavity growth and subsequent cavitation bubble collapse, inducing a transient suction force across a curved, two-radii Young-Laplace capillary boundary. Velocity drops are derived from closed-form analytical equations that explicitly couple vapor volume dynamics with non-linear flow area restriction and fluid drag. The model predicts a maximum boundary layer wall shear stress of 30.06 Pa at the target interface. Crucially, this shear magnitude matches the physical threshold required to mechanically strip surface contaminant boundary layers while remaining below the damage threshold of underlying target substrates. Finally, we formulate a closed-form expression for the maximum allowable liquid inlet temperature required to prevent thermal saturation and sustain stable, continuous microfluidic suction cycles. These equations establish direct engineering design rules for optimizing phase-change microfluidic actuators and next-generation coaxial fluidic systems.

title: TwinLight: A Multi-Timescale Physical-Layer-Aware T-API-Compliant Optical Domain Controller Digital Twin
comment: Demonstration presented at ECOC 2026, Málaga, Spain, Sept. 2026. Paper ID Tu2-Ex1/1440. Code in https://github.com/carlosnatalino/TwinLight
summary: We demonstrate TwinLight, an open-source optical-network digital twin acting as an optical domain controller. Its T-API REST and telemetry streaming interfaces expose a physical-layer engine that combines a GNPy steady-state baseline with four analytical transients.

title: Breathers across the Focusing-to-Defocusing Transition: From Diffraction-Like Dynamics to Talbot Carpets
summary: We experimentally investigate fundamental unstable breather wave groups propagating across the transition from focusing to defocusing regimes. In hydrodynamics, this transition is realized through a rapid reduction in water depth over a short spatial interval. We demonstrate that the time-periodic Akhmediev breather develops a Talbot-like recurrence pattern in the defocusing regime, although only its initial stages are experimentally accessible. In contrast, the Peregrine breather exhibits qualitatively different behavior, characterized by oscillatory envelope dynamics. These oscillations can be understood as a purely linear phenomenon arising within the nonlinear Schrödinger framework when dispersion dominates over nonlinearity, as further confirmed by numerical simulations over extended propagation distances. The experimental observations agree closely with finite-depth nonlinear Schrödinger predictions across regimes with substantially different relative strengths of dispersion and nonlinearity. Our findings reveal a temporal analogue of diffraction and provide a foundation for exploring focusing-to-defocusing transitions in other nonlinear dispersive media.

title: Redetermination of the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients of BaMgF4
summary: BaMgF4 (BMF) has the potential to serve as a platform material for vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) nonlinear optics owing to its ferroelectricity and high UV transparency down to 130 nm. However, the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients reported for BMF span approximately one order of magnitude, hindering a reliable assessment of its potential for nonlinear optical applications. Here, we redetermined these coefficients by combining Maker fringe, wedge, and single-pass second-harmonic-generation measurements at a fundamental wavelength of 1064 nm. Our results establish that all the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients of BMF lie in the range of 0.01-0.04 pm/V. We determined d31 to be 0.035 pm/V, which is among the largest coefficients of BMF, while it has been underestimated relative to the other coefficients in previous studies. Although d31 is not the largest coefficient, the use of its long corresponding coherence length is beneficial for quasi-phase matching, particularly for VUV generation, where the fabrication of lower-order quasi-phase-matching structures is crucial.

title: Evaporation-induced colloidal diffusiophoresis in electrolyte solutions
summary: Non-volatile solutes accumulate near a receding drying front, generating concentration gradients that can drive directional colloidal transport by diffusiophoresis. This dynamic spatial arrangement of colloidal particles could affect the microstructure and macroscopic properties of the dried film. Here, we combine experiments and theory to investigate polystyrene particles suspended in electrolyte solutions drying within a capillary tube. By varying the electrolyte composition and ambient relative humidity, we show that evaporation-induced ion gradients drive particles toward the liquid-gas interface and enhance interfacial accumulation, whereas slower drying at higher humidity weakens the gradient and particle migration. We use the heat balance integral method to predict the transient solute field for a receding interface and couple it to particle transport to capture the observed particle trajectories and accumulation trends. These results identify background electrolytes and drying rate as coupled controls on particle distribution and provide a predictive framework to optimize formulation and processing parameters for manufacturing slurry-based materials, such as battery electrodes and turbine coatings.

title: When is an Optical Design Problem a Mass Transfer Problem?
summary: This paper investigates whether optical design problems can be represented as Monge--Kantorovich mass transfer problems with some cost function. An optical problem is specified by a function defining a particular family of supporting surfaces for the optical element. We introduce the notion of geometric equivalence between optical and transport problems, which is directly related to the possibility of formulating an optical design problem as a mass transfer problem. A necessary condition for such equivalence is derived in the semi-discrete setting. It allows a transport representation to be ruled out without choosing a cost function in advance. The condition is applied to the near-field refractor problem and to the design of two refracting surfaces transforming a spherical beam into a spherical or collimated beam. For these problems, the necessary condition is shown to fail in physically admissible configurations. We also study an optical element with a single working surface and an arbitrary regular incident wavefront. In the far field, geometric equivalence to a mass transfer problem requires a planar or spherical wavefront, whereas in the near field with a planar target, the necessary condition fails for an arbitrary smooth wavefront.

title: An acousto-optic colorimeter for color psychophysics
summary: A complete model of human color perception requires the ability to present any color as a stimulus.Most existing measurements were collected with physical color samples, and current laboratory generators, such as displays and multi-primary LED systems, work with a small number of fixed primaries. Published color-difference data therefore cover about 40\% of the CIE~$xy$ chromaticity diagram, while commercial wide-gamut displays already reach two thirds of it and need difference metrics there. We describe an acousto-optic colorimeter that lets the experimenter choose the primaries. The device selects up to four narrow bands from a supercontinuum (white-light) laser, each with electronically set wavelength and intensity, and covers 95\% of the CIE~$xy$ chromaticity diagram. Threshold-scale color differences, presented in alternation as in a discrimination experiment, are reproduced with a mean error of 0.08--0.12 CIEDE2000 units ($ΔE_{00}$) at five CIE-recommended color centers. Because one color can be built from many combinations of narrow bands, the bands are chosen for the task: the finest adjustment for color matching, the least disagreement between observers for color-difference measurement. In simulations with 151~individual observers from a published dataset, with these bands observers see colors 0.6--1.9~$ΔE_{00}$ from the intended one on average, against 1.2--2.5~$ΔE_{00}$ on a calibrated wide-gamut LCD, lower at every center. The approach applies to any narrowband source and lets experimenters use saturated colors while limiting the effect of individual differences in color vision.

title: Raytracing and quantifying the inferior mirage
summary: Using custom raytracing code, we explore several features of the inferior mirage that are not widely discussed, such as the blurring in the mirage image, and what happens to the light in the direct image region that is replaced by the mirage image. The raytracing model also clarifies how to quantify the mirage, and we provide expressions to calculate the angular extent of the mirage under given thermal conditions and measurement geometry.

title: Optical microscopy for pathological imaging: past, present, and future
summary: Histopathology, the microscopic examination of stained tissue sections, remains the gold standard for pathology imaging, but its bright-field imaging is largely morphological. Advanced optical microscopy techniques move beyond this by exploiting diverse light-matter interactions, and are increasingly applied to pathological imaging. By capturing signals such as refractive index, polarisation, harmonic generation, Brillouin shift, and molecular vibrations, these microscopy techniques can provide quantitative or semi-quantitative information on tissue structure, mechanics, and chemical or molecular composition. In this review, we summarise the physical principles, key quantitative parameters, and representative pathological applications of seven modalities--optical diffraction tomography, polarisation microscopy, second-harmonic generation microscopy, third-harmonic generation microscopy, Brillouin microscopy, Raman microscopy, and fluorescence microscopy. We also discuss progress in artificial intelligence that supports reconstruction, analysis, and interpretation across these modalities, together with emerging trends in multimodal integration. Overall, this review shows how different optical contrasts can complement routine histopathology, while outlining the challenges and opportunities that will shape their clinical translation.

title: Self-injection-locked dark-soliton Kerr optical frequency combs with high even-order normal dispersion
comment: 4 pages, 4 figures, to be published in Optics Letters
summary: We numerically investigate dissipative dark-soliton (DDS) microcombs under the action of pure high even-order normal (HEON) dispersion in a microresonator with the self-injection locking (SIL). Pure 4th, 6th, 10th, and 14th-order normal dispersion can support DDSs formed by interlocked switching waves, directly excited through a SIL-based turnkey scheme without detuning sweeps. Compared to the pure 4th-order case, the switching-wave tail oscillation period increases and its decay rate decreases with the increase of the dispersion order. Although the overall comb bandwidth narrows, the number of non-pump comb lines above a common absolute power threshold increases. Furthermore, the feedback phase controls the DDS duty cycle and intracavity comb-line power distribution, while the increase of the pump power improves the estimated pump-to-comb output conversion efficiency.

title: Differential chiral sensing at exceptional points in intrinsically chiral metastructures
summary: Discriminating opposite enantiomers through their weak chiroptical responses remains a fundamental challenge in optical sensing. Exceptional points (EPs), non-Hermitian singularities at which eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce, offer a route to enhanced spectral responses through their characteristic square-root eigenvalue splitting. However, their potential for chiral discrimination remains largely unexplored. We demonstrate exceptional points in an intrinsically chiral hybrid metamaterial and reveal strongly asymmetric responses to enantiomeric perturbations. The interplay between intrinsic chirality and non-Hermitian degeneracy is realized through the coupling of a chiral plasmonic nanoantenna array to a photonic crystal slab. We observe characteristic complex-square-root scaling, with both resonance frequencies and loss-rates exhibiting pronounced handedness dependence. Remarkably, opposite enantiomers produce complex mode splittings that differ by more than an order of magnitude. Our findings establish intrinsic chirality as a new degree of freedom in non-Hermitian physics and reveal a fundamental route toward topological singularities enhanced discrimination of chiral matter.

title: Laser-Direct-Written polymer WGM microring laser integrated on a fiber tip for refractive index sensing
summary: Whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microlasers are promising for refractometric sensing, but their practical implementation can be limited by the need for stable resonator-coupler alignment. Here, we demonstrate a Rhodamine B-doped polymer WGM microring laser directly fabricated on an optical-fiber tip, eliminating the external resonator-fiber coupling interface at the sensing head. Micro-droplet coating and UV laser direct writing are combined for fabrication, while finite-difference time-domain simulations guide the microring laser design. The microlasers operate in air and water with thresholds of 0.224 uJ and 0.458 uJ, respectively. Refractometric measurements in aqueous glucose solutions yield a bulk refractive index sensitivity of 364.95 nm/RIU and a detection limit of 2.47 x 10^(-4) RIU. Water-induced polymer changes and photobleaching are also investigated. This fiber-tip architecture provides a basis for probe-based refractometric sensing in environmental and biochemical applications.

title: Deep-UV All-dielectric qBIC Metasurface for Refractive Index Sensing
summary: All-dielectric metasurfaces supporting quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs) have emerged as powerful platforms for biosensing, yet their operation remains largely concentrated in the visible and near-infrared regimes. Extending these resonances into the deep-ultraviolet (DUV) to probe the intrinsic electronic absorption of biomolecules presents substantial material and nanofabrication challenges. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a hafnium dioxide (HfO$_{2}$) metasurface supporting DUV qBICs in the wavelength range from 225 nm to 340 nm with quality factors reaching 500. We further demonstrate its refractive index sensing capabilities through integration with a microfluidic cell and optical characterization in reflection mode. We show that the introduction of an aqueous buffer leads to a further quality factor enhancement. Achieving a sensitivity of up to approximately 60 nm/RIU and an operational figure of merit of 40 $\mathrm{RIU}^{-1}$, this low-loss HfO$_{2}$ metasurface provides a robust foundation for label-free DUV biosensing.

title: Modulation Induced Memory Resonances in Dynamically Driven Optical Cavities
summary: Temporal modulation of optical cavities provides a powerful mechanism for controlling photonic states beyond the static cavity paradigm. Here, we investigate the dynamics of periodically driven optical cavities using a time-dependent cavity-field model with modulated resonance frequencies. We demonstrate modulation-induced tuning of cavity resonances and analyze the resulting intracavity field evolution in both amplitude and phase. The interplay between periodic modulation and cavity dissipation gives rise to pronounced hysteretic behavior, revealing memory effects associated with the finite photon lifetime of the cavity. By quantifying the hysteresis area as a function of modulation frequency, we identify distinct memory resonances characterized by enhanced field-history dependence at specific driving frequencies. Furthermore, we examine the time-resolved local density of optical states (LDOS) and show that temporal modulation enables dynamic spectral redistribution of photonic states, with the degree of confinement governed by the cavity loss rate. Our results establish a simple framework for understanding and engineering memory effects in dynamically driven optical resonators and provide new opportunities for tunable photonic environments, dynamic LDOS control, and reconfigurable light-matter interactions.

title: Tailoring resonator geometry for astigmatism compensation with structured light in birefringent optical cavities
summary: In this work, we experimentally investigate the astigmatism induced by a birefringent crystal inside an optical cavity and demonstrate a geometric compensation strategy for structured modes carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM). We show that the astigmatism observed in the semimonolithic configuration can be fully compensated by introducing a third mirror to fold the cavity, thereby exploiting the geometric astigmatism arising from oblique incidence on the curved mirror. By performing a study of the resonator geometry, both theoretical and experimental results confirm that this approach enables the preservation of OAM between the pump beam and the converted signal and idler modes, providing an effective design strategy for birefringent optical cavities.

title: Discrete time crystals and heteroclinic switching in actively mode-locked semiconductor lasers
comment: 10 figures, 25 pages, submitted to Chaos Soliton and Fractals (special issue dedicated to Andrei Vladimirov)
summary: We investigate the mechanisms underlying the emergence of discrete time crystals in actively mode-locked semiconductor lasers. Our analysis is based on a Haus master equation generalized to retain carrier memory between round-trips. We perform a detailed bifurcation analysis that reveals a well-defined hierarchy of subharmonic states, illustrating how pulses may suppress their neighbors when the modulation runs faster than the pulse round-trip frequency. To identify the underlying mechanism, we derive effective equations of motion that couple the pulse energies, their positions relative to the modulation transmission maxima, and the local time-dependent gain. These reveal that transitions between time-crystalline states occur via transcritical global bifurcations, opening a regime of heteroclinic winnerless competition between symmetry-degenerate configurations.

title: Universal photonic synthetic temporal-mode converter for heterogeneous quantum interconnects
summary: We propose a synthetic temporal-mode converter (STC) that combines programmable waveform matching with denser time multiplexing for heterogeneous quantum interconnects. Programmable couplers and optical delays reshape known single-photon temporal waveforms through coherent interference between time bins. Conversion to a common single-bin mode concentrates amplitudes from $N$ bins in $\lceil\log_2N\rceil$ mixing stages, simultaneously improving temporal indistinguishability and freeing channel time. Simulations yield mode overlaps above 99.9\% for exponential and Gaussian inputs. For $N=256$ and $0.5\,\mathrm{dB}$ loss per stage, STC gives a 45.6-fold higher photon-pair coincidence rate than temporal gating at equal mode overlap for two exponential inputs. Relative to long pulses, the shortened temporal matched mode can support an approximately 41-fold higher photon-pair coincidence rate when the available time-multiplexing capacity is fully utilized.

title: Shaping Frequency-Bin Biphoton Correlations via Programmable Optical Frequency Combs
summary: Programmable shaping of photon-pair spectral correlations is important for frequency-bin quantum information processing. However, achieving this control remains challenging in nonlinear optical systems without reliable forward models. Here, we demonstrate model-free, hardware-in-the-loop shaping of the measured joint spectral intensity of a cascaded photon-pair source driven by a programmable optical frequency comb. A blockwise simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation controller optimizes up to 22 pump, signal, and idler parameters. Each iteration requires only two accepted hardware evaluations, independent of the parameter count. The controller converges to diverse target patterns on 3$\times$3, 4$\times$4, and 5$\times$5 frequency-bin grids. The optimized distributions achieve Pearson correlations between 0.66 and 0.98 and classical overlap fidelities between 0.32 and 0.62. Cross-target similarity analysis confirms that the optimized patterns remain target-specific. Source characterization yields a maximum coincidence-to-accidental ratio of approximately 585. Accuracy is limited by pump-phase transfer, parasitic nonlinear background, waveshaper constraints, amplitude-only filtering, and measurement noise. Joint spectral intensity contains no spectral-phase information. Therefore, the results demonstrate control of measured frequency-bin populations and correlations, not complete reconstruction of the two-photon state. Phase-sensitive characterization is required to verify inter-bin coherence and quantify the entanglement dimensionality of the output state. Our results establish direct measurement feedback as a practical approach to reconfigurable frequency-bin correlation engineering when an accurate end-to-end model is unavailable.

title: Cavity-enhanced second harmonic generation from Rydberg excitons in Cu$_2$O
summary: Rydberg excitons in Cu$_2$O provide a solid-state setting for creating giant optical nonlinearities. Here, we use second-harmonic generation (SHG) to study Rydberg excitons in a doubly resonant optical microcavity designed to enhance both the pump and second-harmonic fields. We observe even-parity exciton states in an optical cavity and extend cavity-based measurements of Rydberg excitons up to $n=10$. The SHG intensity depends strongly on pump cavity detuning, showing the dominant role of the microcavity is the enhancement of the intra-cavity pump field. Analysis reveals an additional enhancement from the resonant second-harmonic cavity giving an overall SHG enhancement factor of $21 \pm 2$ inside the microcavity. These results establish cavity-enhanced SHG spectroscopy as a valuable tool for studying Rydberg excitons in microcavities and provide a pathway towards exploiting optical nonlinearities in Rydberg exciton polariton systems.

title: Inversion symmetry breaking by interlayer hybridization in a tetralayer van der Waals heterostructure
summary: Inversion symmetry breaking unlocks a broad range of physical phenomena fundamental for modern technologies, motivating efforts to engineer noncentrosymmetric materials. In this context, monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides, which naturally lack inversion symmetry, have emerged as a versatile platform for valley physics, strong excitonic effects, and nonlinear optics. However, in their hexagonal stacking phase, inversion symmetry is restored in even-layer stacks and bulk form, suppressing these effects and limiting applications. In this work, inversion symmetry breaking is demonstrated in a vertically stacked tetralayer heterostructure assembled from two intrinsically centrosymmetric bilayer flakes, as evidenced by second harmonic generation measurements with an intensity comparable to that of their constituent monolayer. Spectroscopic measurements and theoretical estimations indicate that effective symmetry breaking in the tetralayer heterostructure is driven by interlayer hybridization, giving rise to pronounced electronic and phononic signatures. This symmetry breaking further induces polar anisotropy, with an intensity ratio reaching 2.36.
